text: I’ll model the stated radii as smooth cosine blends on each half of the 0.9 m duct, giving zero axial slope at the inlet, mid-plane, and outlet. The fluid region is the annular volume between those two revolved profiles. I’ll first create a coarse CAD representation and inspect its dimensions and shape; after that I’ll export explicitly named patch surfaces and mesh the closed volume. All coordinates will be authored directly in metres.

The coarse CAD will use nine circular sections along the axis, sampled from the cosine laws. A smooth OCC loft joins each set of sections; subtracting the core loft from the outer loft creates the bypass-air solid. This is intentionally low-resolution in the axial direction so the overall topology and scale can be checked before surface tessellation and meshing.

The first loft attempt did not build; the likely issue is the section-wire orientation produced by the plane transform. I’ll inspect a few transformed circles before retrying, rather than carrying an invalid CAD object forward.
I’ll repeat the inspection using only supported shape properties.

I’ll switch to the more robust construction for a surface of revolution: one closed meridional spline profile in the axial–radial plane, revolved 360° about the engine axis. This directly creates the annular fluid solid and avoids loft seam compatibility. The cell redefines all parameters and helpers so it is reproducible from an empty directory.

The coarse view shows the intended single annular passage with four boundary faces. I’ll now tessellate those four surfaces from the same cosine radius functions and shared boundary rings, naming each patch at creation: `outerCowl`, `coreCowl`, `fanExitInlet`, and `nozzleOutlet`. The tessellation uses 48 axial intervals and 96 circumferential intervals; all vertices remain in metres, and triangle winding is outward from the fluid.

I’ll use `snappyHexMesh` on a coarse Cartesian background grid. The keep-point is inside the bypass annulus at `(0.45, 0, 0.37)` m. The background box extends 50 mm beyond the duct in the axial direction and 50 mm beyond the maximum cowl radius radially; its temporary boundary lies outside the retained closed region and should disappear after trimming. Surface refinement level 1 is the initial coarse mesh.
The meshing dictionaries are ready. I’ll now generate the coarse background mesh and run the coarse surface-conforming cut/snap pass, capturing each log separately.
`blockMesh` rejected the dictionary before creating a mesh. I’ll inspect its log to correct the specific syntax error.

The mesh dictionary itself was not reached; OpenFOAM requires a minimal `controlDict` even for preprocessing utilities. I’ll add only that required case metadata, without solver or boundary-condition setup.
With the required case metadata present, I’ll rerun the coarse mesh generation.
The background grid now builds, but `snappyHexMesh` rejected its configuration. I’ll inspect the relevant end of that log.

This OpenFOAM build also initializes standard case dictionaries before preprocessing. I’ll add empty `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries; they contain no solver setup and only satisfy utility startup.
I’ll rerun both mesh stages so the accepted build sequence remains reproducible from empty.
The utility now reads the case and has reached a later configuration issue; I’ll inspect the new log tail.
`snappyHexMesh` expects the standard discretization sub-dictionaries even though it will not solve equations. I’ll provide empty/default preprocessing-safe sections only.
I’ll rerun the two meshing stages with the corrected startup dictionaries.
The preprocessing startup now passes; I’ll inspect the remaining `snappyHexMeshDict` compatibility error.
OpenFOAM 2512 requires an explicit, even if empty, `refinementRegions` dictionary. I’ll add it to the castellated controls.
I’ll rerun the reproducible background and snapping stages after that version-specific correction.
The coarse snap completed without meshing-stage quality errors. I’ll now run the binding `checkMesh` assessment and report the cell count, topology, geometry, and worst quality values.

The exhaustive geometry mode flags 744 concave polyhedra, so I will not accept this coarse mesh as final. Before changing the strategy, I’ll run the standard binding form of `checkMesh` to confirm whether the same defect is considered fatal there.

The standard `checkMesh` passes: 27,428 cells, four patches, 46.95° maximum non-orthogonality, 1.07 maximum skewness, and 0.28747 m³ mesh volume versus 0.28856 m³ CAD volume. I’ll now load the actual OpenFOAM mesh and render its boundary plus an axial cut so the retained annulus and patch coverage can be visually checked.

The rendered OpenFOAM mesh shows the annular passage retained correctly and all four named patches covering their intended surfaces. I’ll perform a final numerical patch audit from the actual mesh: patch face counts, bounds, and inlet/outlet axial locations.

The patch audit reveals a coarse-grid edge-labeling artifact: `snappyHexMesh` assigned a narrow row of adjacent cowl faces to each end patch (about 14–15 mm axial spill). The geometry is closed and the mesh passes, but the inlet/outlet patch separation should be sharper. I’ll inspect actual boundary-face normal components to establish a robust normal-based correction rather than using a bounding-box rule.

The normal distributions confirm that the end patches are distinct—the end faces have \(|n_x| \ge 0.725\), while cowl faces are predominantly near radial—but the coarse cut cells bridge the geometric corner. I’ll refine all four surfaces one additional level (nominal boundary cell size about 10 mm) to reduce that edge spill while retaining a moderate mesh size.
I’ll rebuild from the Cartesian background and run the refined snapping pass.
The refined mesh completed cleanly. I’ll rerun standard `checkMesh` and refresh the patch audit from the new mesh.

The final refinement reduces end-patch spill to about 5 mm and improves quality: 138,032 cells, 41.38° maximum non-orthogonality, 1.15 maximum skewness, and 0.28824 m³ mesh volume. I’ll now inspect the generated build script and case inventory to ensure the accepted sequence can replay from empty and that exactly the four requested STL patch files are present.

The case contains exactly the four requested STL files and a complete `constant/polyMesh`. I’ll perform one final surface-union audit directly on those STLs: welded-edge closure, triangle winding consistency, sampled radii at the three specified stations, and zero-slope smooth-blend values.
